Reservation schema

  • PostgreSQL defines primary keys as unique, non-null row identifiers and foreign keys as references to existing keys. The example uses both on the claim's slot ID. Modeling one slot as one bookable place is a decision about appointments. Constraints
  • PostgreSQL checks a unique index against concurrent inserts. If the other transaction is still open, its commit or rollback can change the outcome. The exercise observes this wait using the blocking session's process ID. Index uniqueness checks and session information functions.
  • PostgreSQL supports a conflict target and returns rows affected by an insert. At Read Committed, a conflicting row can prevent insertion before it is visible to that statement's snapshot. The example reads the owner in the next statement. Treating a matching attempt as a replay and a different claim as SlotTaken is the application's policy. INSERT and transaction isolation.

Evaluating an index

  • PostgreSQL uses statistics to estimate how many rows a predicate will match. The lab refreshes statistics in both schemas before comparing estimates with actual rows. ANALYZE.
  • A measured plan reports actual rows, loops, execution time and buffer accesses. In this exercise we compare the top node's buffers across plans and use child nodes to locate the work. Using EXPLAIN.
  • Each additional index must stay synchronized with writes. We time a committed insert batch and use pg_relation_size to report the candidate index's main fork in bytes. Workload frequency and the decision to keep it are local judgments. Index introduction and object size functions.

Schema migrations

  • A row-level BEFORE INSERT trigger can change the row before PostgreSQL checks constraints. The exercise uses one to copy a booking identity supplied by either client into the other column. CREATE TRIGGER.
  • Adding a check with NOT VALID enforces it on subsequent inserts and updates. Validating it later scans existing rows with a weaker lock than the one used to add it. The exercise commits validation before requesting the stronger cutover lock. ALTER TABLE.
  • PostgreSQL can replace a view's defining query while preserving its existing output columns. The v2 client keeps the same read interface as its data source changes from both columns to booked_by_id alone. CREATE VIEW.
  • PostgreSQL exposes connected sessions and their application names. Before retiring v1, the playbook checks those observations against API and worker revisions, job schedules and retry lifetimes. Activity statistics.
